analysis.one_liner: Applies the Social Security payroll tax to earnings above the annual cap and uses the money to raise benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill, sponsored by one House Democrat with nine Democratic cosponsors, never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 2023-24 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would phase in Social Security payroll taxes on wages above the annual cap — the cutoff (roughly $160,000-170,000) above which earnings currently go untaxed — until all earnings above it are taxed by 2029. The revenue would fund bigger checks: a higher replacement rate for the first band of a worker's earnings, a 5% credit on above-cap earnings, a cost-of-living index built around what retirees actually buy, larger widow and widower benefits, and a guarantee that the higher checks don't cut Supplemental Security Income for the poorest beneficiaries. The bill was referred to two House committees in May 2023 and never moved again; in its final weeks, the 118th Congress passed it down to subcommittees, and it expired when the session ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future retirees and disabled workers, especially lower earners, whose first band of average earnings would be replaced at 95% instead of 90%, with the dollar amount of that band rising up to 15% by 2044. Widows and widowers in two-income households would get a benefit equal to the greater of their own benefit plus 75% of the deceased spouse's, or the deceased spouse's full benefit. SSI recipients would keep the higher Social Security checks without losing SSI. High earners would get a small new benefit credit too, since 5% of their above-cap earnings would count toward their benefit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees, disabled workers, widows, SSI recipients

how_it_helps.text: Raises the factor that replaces the first band of a worker's average indexed monthly earnings from 90% to 95%, phased in from 2029 to 2033, and increases the dollar amount of that first band by 1% a year up to 15% by 2044 — a larger boost proportionally for lower earners.

Phases in payroll taxation of earnings above the annual cap: 20% of above-cap earnings become taxable in 2025, rising 20 percentage points a year until all of it is taxable in 2029, bringing substantial new revenue into the Social Security trust funds.
Creates a Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers and uses it to calculate Social Security cost-of-living adjustments, so annual raises would track prices seniors actually face.

Changes widow's and widower's benefits for two-income households to the greater of the deceased spouse's full benefit or 75% of the survivor's benefit plus the deceased's, capped at the benefit of a hypothetical average earner — addressing a long-standing gap where survivors of two-earner couples got only one benefit.
Holds SSI beneficiaries harmless: higher Social Security benefits under the bill would not reduce or end their Supplemental Security Income.
Gives high earners a small stake in the new taxes: 5% of their above-cap earnings would count toward their benefit calculation for people first eligible after 2029.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and self-employed people whose earnings exceed the annual Social Security wage cap, and their employers, would pay the payroll tax on all earnings above it, phased in from 2025 through 2028. The employee and employer each pay the tax on the newly covered wages, so highly paid professionals and the businesses employing them bear the cost. High earners recoup only a fraction through the 5% surplus-earnings benefit credit.

drawbacks.text: It is a large tax increase on households and businesses with earnings above the wage cap: the payroll tax would eventually apply to every dollar of earnings, not just the first roughly $160,000-170,000.

The offsetting benefit for high earners is small by design — 5% of above-cap earnings count toward benefits — so high earners would pay far more in taxes than they receive back, which critics would call a redistribution financed on a narrow tax base.

The benefit expansions are permanent and start while the above-cap tax is still phasing in; the record provided contains no cost estimate, so whether the new revenue fully covers the higher bend points, the elderly CPI, the widow and widower changes, and the SSI hold-harmless cannot be verified from this record.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is broad and progressive: bigger checks for lower earners, more accurate inflation adjustments for seniors, a fix for surviving spouses of two-earner couples, and protection for the poorest beneficiaries on SSI. The cost is concentrated on the top slice of earners and their employers, which is the bill's point — that is who currently escapes the tax above the cap. The honest caveat is fiscal: the bill never received a cost estimate, so whether the above-cap tax fully pays for the permanent benefit expansions is unproven in the record, and a program already projected to face a funding shortfall decades out would be taking on large new obligations on the strength of a new revenue stream.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means Committee for the entire two-year Congress without a hearing or markup, was passed down to subcommittees in the closing weeks, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Linda Sánchez introduced the bill on May 11, 2023, joined by nine other House Democrats as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced, the standard first step that puts a bill in committee's hands.

No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred; the only further action came on December 17, 2024, in the Congress's final weeks, when it was referred to the Social Security and Work and Welfare subcommittees — a step that typically signals the end of the road rather than the beginning of consideration.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired with it, as any bill not passed does when a Congress ends.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners and the businesses employing them are better off, because the payroll tax on earnings above the cap never materialized. Social Security's financing challenge is also untouched, since no alternative passed instead.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners who never paid the new tax

for.name: Rep. Linda T. Sánchez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled the Democratic cosponsor group.

for.name: Nine House Democrats (Reps. Pocan, Schakowsky, Lee of California, Cartwright, Lofgren, Lynch, Pingree, Norton, and Cohen)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no member of either party added their name afterward.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of primary jurisdiction over Social Security
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for the full two-year Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote, and referred it to a subcommittee in the Congress's final weeks.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; the record shows no action beyond referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and because the bill never reached the floor, no one in either party ever recorded a vote on it.

industries.industry: High earners above the Social Security wage cap
industries.note: The bill would phase in the payroll tax on all earnings above the annual cap, eventually taxing every dollar of high wages and self-employment income. The offsetting gain — 5% of above-cap earnings counting toward benefits — is small relative to the new taxes, so this group's interest in the bill runs against the beneficiaries the bill funds.
Employers pay a matching share of Social Security payroll taxes, so businesses with highly paid staff would owe the tax on the newly covered wages above the cap once it is phased in.
